source: USDA ARS Tree Fruit Research Laboratory / Washington State University Extension Tree Fruit IPM
title: Peach Leaf Curl (Taphrina deformans, Ascomycota Taphrinaceae) on Peach and Nectarine
content: Peach leaf curl is the most common and most important spring fungal disease of peach (Prunus persica L. Batsch) and nectarine (P. persica var. nucipersica) worldwide, caused by the dimorphic ascomycete Taphrina deformans (Berk.) Tul. (subphylum Taphrinomycotina, class Taphrinomycetes, order Taphrinales, family Taphrinaceae). The disease occurs in all peach and nectarine growing regions of North America, South America, Europe, the Mediterranean basin, South Africa, China, Japan, Australia, and New Zealand; it is most severe in areas with cool, wet spring weather during the peach budbreak and leaf expansion period. Yield losses of 20-90% are documented in unsprayed susceptible peach cultivars during years with extended spring rainfall. In addition to direct fruit yield reduction, severe repeated infections cause 30-70% premature defoliation, reduced fruit size and soluble sugar content, fruit surface blemishes rendering fruit unmarketable for fresh sale, reduced flower bud set and fruitfulness for the following growing season, reduced tree vigor and winter cold-hardiness, and increased tree susceptibility to secondary Cytospora canker, bacterial canker (Pseudomonas syringae pv. syringae), and brown rot blossom blight. Almond (P. dulcis), apricot (P. armeniaca), and plum (P. domestica, P. salicina) are occasionally infected but are generally considered tolerant or resistant compared to peach and nectarine. The diagnostic symptom of peach leaf curl develops on newly emerged young leaves 2-3 weeks after budbreak: the young leaves are thickened, distorted, puckered, curled downward and inward, and develop a characteristic reddish, purplish, or bright yellowish-red discoloration on the upper surface. As the distorted leaves expand, the entire leaf blade becomes severely deformed, twisted, curled, and brittle; the thickened reddish leaf surface develops a grayish, powdery, velvety bloom of asci and ascospores of the T. deformans ascogenous stage approximately 10-14 days after first symptoms appear (this powdery gray bloom is diagnostic, distinguishing leaf curl from aphid feeding injury, peach rosette mosaic virus, or nutrient deficiency). Severely infected young leaves usually turn brown, wither, and drop prematurely from the tree within 2-4 weeks of symptom development; this early defoliation triggers production of replacement leaves from latent adventitious buds, which are usually free of curl symptoms because temperatures have warmed and infection is no longer possible. In addition to leaves, young succulent shoots, green twigs, petioles, and young developing fruit can also be infected: infected young shoots are swollen, thickened, shortened, stunted, and develop a yellowish-green to reddish-purple discoloration; the terminal portion of heavily infected new shoots often dies back (dieback), providing entry courts for Cytospora and Leucostoma canker fungi. Fruit symptoms appear as small, reddish, raised, warty, rough-textured, corky lesions 3-15 mm in diameter on green immature fruit; fruit lesions may crack open as the fruit expands, allowing entry of secondary Monilinia brown rot, Rhizopus soft rot, and Penicillium blue mold decay fungi. Taphrina deformans overwinters in two forms: (1) the saprotrophic yeast-like budding (anamorphic) blastospore stage (formerly classified as the genus 'Cryptococcus' or 'Pullularia' but now recognized as the mitosporic state of T. deformans) survives epiphytically on the surface of peach and nectarine bark surfaces, within bud scales, in bark crevices, and on the surface of dormant buds. (2) The haploid mycelial stage may also persist in minute lesions in the outer bark tissue of 1-year-old wood. In the spring, during the period of bud swell (pink tip stage) through budbreak and early leaf expansion (approximately 10-day window in the northeastern US), the overwintered yeast-like blastospores on bud scales are activated by temperatures of 10-19 C and splashed by rainwater onto the surfaces of newly emerging, tender, unexpanded leaf primordia, young shoot apices, and fruit initials. The yeast-like cells are capable of mating (conjugation of compatible haploid cells via a conjugation tube) to form dikaryotic infection hyphae that penetrate the host directly through the thin, unprotected cuticle of very young expanding leaves (before the cuticular wax layer has fully developed), through young petioles, or through stomata on still-expanding leaf surfaces. Infection requires 3-14 mm of rain (or overhead sprinkler irrigation water) providing continuous free moisture on the bud and young leaf surfaces for 12-48 hours at temperatures of 5-20 C; the minimum temperature for infection is 1 C (34 F), the optimum temperature is 12-18 C (54-64 F), and no infection occurs above 26 C (79 F), explaining why the disease is exclusively a problem of early spring cool wet weather in all production areas. Once inside the young host tissue, the dikaryotic mycelium grows intercellularly and subcuticularly producing characteristic hypertrophy (cell enlargement) and hyperplasia (excessive cell division) of the palisade and spongy mesophyll cells, resulting in the thickened, distorted, reddish, curled leaf morphology. After approximately 10-14 days of intercellular growth, the dikaryotic mycelium breaks through the lower leaf epidermis and the palisade layer and forms a palisade layer of naked asci (ascogenous hymenium) directly on the upper and lower leaf surface; this is the characteristic grayish 'powdery' bloom stage. Each ascus (30-80 x 10-15 um, cylindrical to club-shaped) contains 8 (rarely 4) ellipsoidal, hyaline, uninucleate haploid ascospores (4-8 x 3-5 um); ascospores are forcibly discharged from the asci by turgor pressure during rain and are wind-dispersed or splash-dispersed back onto the bark surface and developing bud scales of the same tree, where they immediately convert back to the saprotrophic budding yeast-like stage that will survive the following dormant season. Notably, there is only ONE primary infection cycle per growing season; there are no secondary cycles of reinfection in summer, which explains why the later replacement leaves that develop after mid-spring are usually always symptomless. Management: (1) dormant-season fungicide application is the single most effective, reliable, and standard management practice for peach leaf curl worldwide. A single fungicide spray applied between 90% leaf fall in late autumn (November) and dormant delayed-dormant / 'pink bud' stage in early spring (immediately before bud scales break and green tissue emerges - this is the last effective spray timing) will provide 95-100% control of T. deformans even under the most severe infection pressure. The single most effective material for dormant leaf curl control for > 130 years has been lime sulfur (calcium polysulfide, commercial formulations of 29% sulfur as CaSx) applied at 2-4 gallons per 100 gallons dilute (6-8% v/v, or 22-44 g sulfur per liter); Bordeaux mixture (copper sulfate + hydrated lime, classical 8:8:100 formulation, 8 lbs copper sulfate + 8 lbs hydrated lime per 100 gal water) is the second most effective dormant material and is permitted in certified organic production. In recent decades, dormant applications of fixed copper formulations (copper hydroxide, copper oxychloride, tribasic copper sulfate, copper ammonium complex, Bordeaux-type copper-lime dusts) at equivalent metallic copper rates of 2-4 lb metallic Cu per acre have shown equivalent efficacy to lime sulfur. After green leaf tissue has emerged, copper and lime sulfur sprays may cause phytotoxic russeting and leaf necrosis, so they must be applied before green tip. (2) post-infection foliar fungicide sprays are generally NOT effective for peach leaf curl: once the characteristic reddish curled symptoms are visible, the fungus is already deeply established in the hypertrophied host tissue and no fungicide will remove the symptoms. However, in years when a dormant spray was forgotten or washed off by heavy rain, a foliar application of FRAC 3 DMI triazoles (tebuconazole, difenoconazole, propiconazole, myclobutanil, fenbuconazole, metconazole) or FRAC 11 QoI (azoxystrobin, pyraclostrobin, trifloxystrobin) tank-mixed with FRAC M3 mancozeb applied at the late dormant / bud swell stage (white tip to pink tip) and again at 50% leaf expansion will reduce but not eliminate leaf curl incidence, and will help protect the young fruit from secondary fungal infection. (3) cultural practices: thin fruit to moderate crop load to compensate for partial defoliation; ensure adequate balanced N-P-K fertilization and regular deep watering during summer drought to maintain vigor and support production of replacement leaves; prune out and remove any obviously dead or dying shoots and small branches showing curl-induced dieback during dormant pruning to reduce Cytospora canker infection courts; apply 5-10 cm of organic wood-chip mulch over the root zone; avoid overhead sprinkler irrigation during the spring budbreak period where practical. (4) genetic resistance: peach leaf curl resistance is controlled by a single dominant gene Vr2 (from P. davidiana) and several quantitative trait loci (QTLs). A few commercial peach cultivars with moderate to high partial quantitative resistance are available: 'Elberta' (the classic old canning peach, moderately resistant), 'Redhaven' and its many 'Haven' derivatives ('Glohaven', 'Cresthaven', 'Sunhaven') show good partial resistance; 'Babygold 5', 'Babygold 6', 'Biscoe', 'Harvester', 'Loring', and 'Redskin' are moderately resistant. 'Frost', a white-fleshed peach released by the University of California, carries a high level of monogenic resistance derived from the Chinese landrace 'Chinese Cling'. No commercially important nectarine cultivars carry significant curl resistance; nearly all popular yellow-fleshed and white-fleshed nectarine varieties are highly susceptible and require strict dormant spray programs. (5) biological control: experimental trials with epiphytic antagonist yeasts (Aureobasidium pullulans, Metschnikowia fructicola, Cryptococcus laurentii, Pseudozyma flocculosa) applied at dormancy break have achieved 40-60% curl reduction under moderate disease pressure, but none of these biologicals are yet registered for commercial peach leaf curl use in the US.
